item.title: Benchmark on AGI. If ARC-AGI-3 is solved, do we have AGI?
item.description:
Benchmarks are needed so that an engineer can test their project, look at competitors, and compare themselves to them. Each benchmark has its own purpose.

ARC-AGI-3 was created by the ARC Prize Foundation, founded by François Chollet, to assess general intelligence and the learning ability of AI agents. Complex interactive tasks in the form of games implied that only an artificial intelligence that can explore an unfamiliar world, understand rules on the fly, plan actions, and adapt to new conditions could solve them. That is, it can learn.

A number of projects claim a score of 100% on this benchmark. But that is not a victory. In this article, I analyze why.

Read more

item.title: The evolution of the table in the report: from a summary Excel to a complete picture of the construction project
item.description:
Anyone preparing for a quarterly committee is the last person who wants to hear a question addressed directly to them: "What changed in the money after your management?" or something along the lines of: "What effect did you personally bring to the company?" The cold feeling in the pit of your stomach after those phrases is exactly what shapes a mature manager—though one would hope that growth could happen less dramatically.

The interface style, the direction of the lines, the chart format and design don't matter if they don't let you grasp the "effect" or "damage" for the project and the company within two seconds. In a toxic corporate reality, a number on a callout, a milestone on a graph, the color of a bar, or a table in the legend instead of "additional information" turn into potential hooks for questions. If the answers to them are "...not yet worked out," the speaker already hears in those questions a doubt about the need for further cooperation with them.

As usually happens, the initiative buried the initiator, and a simple list with notes like "what | from where | useful for..." grew into something close to a full-blown study.

Read more

item.title: Four roles of neural networks in photo processing
item.description:
Here is the English translation of the provided Russian text, keeping technical terms as requested. **Translation:**

The phrase "Neural network photo processing" sounds nice and high-tech. Some people are even already tired of it, as they associate it with a stream of neural slop.

But here's the problem. What does it actually mean to process a photo with a neural network? The word "neural network" here is too general a concept, akin to the word "electric motor." And the latter, as we know, works both in an electric car and in a toothbrush.

In the previous two parts, we delved very deeply into the theory and analyzed how AI generally works with images and what pitfalls exist. In this article, we will rise a bit from the depths of theory and look at how real-world problems are solved.

To illustrate everything described, I will use photos I took myself in different years. In addition, I will be helped by several AI tools. My arsenal will include examples from Adobe Photoshop and its Camera Raw add-on, the PortraitPro and Retouch4me plugins, as well as the promising development Evoto.

Important! This is not a tutorial for these tools and certainly not a collection of "what a young neural network artist needs." In this article, we will classify real tools based on the principle of their operation. And the software from the list above will help us illustrate the work.

So. What do a noise reducer and inpainting have in common? Why is it easy to check a mask, but not the result of a generation? And what kind of model is this that requires you to upload five thousand of your frames before it starts to be useful? All answers below.

Read more

item.title: Do transformers dream of electric sheep?
item.description:
In 2015, Google released a series of images that looked as if a photograph had been given to an artist for editing, only they forgot to stop him in time. Dozens of eyes appeared on ordinary landscapes, dogs began to be discernible in the clouds, architecture became covered in repeating patterns, and trees transformed into something between vegetation and an artist's fantasy. The images quickly spread across the internet, and DeepDream fairly soon became a distinct visual style.

Initially, researchers were interested not so much in the images themselves, but in the possibility of understanding what happens inside a neural network. A classifier looks fairly simple from the outside: a photograph is fed into the model, and a list of probabilities comes out — dog, cat, car, airplane. Between these two points lies a huge number of computations, and from a single model output it is often not clear why it arrived at that particular result.

You can look at the activation values of individual neurons and channels, build feature maps, and find images that elicit a strong response. There is also a more radical method of investigation: deliberately altering the input image so that some internal signal of the model becomes stronger. That is how DeepDream came to be.

Read more

item.title: Bookmarklet that calculates the speed of a gguf model in llama.cpp on hf
item.description:
With the advent of neural networks, problems can now be solved much more easily, although such problems would not have existed without neural networks, llama.cpp, and Hugging Face. In general, the point of the article is to attempt to mathematically calculate the theoretical token generation speed in the llama.cpp program for models on Hugging Face, simply by opening the model card and clicking on a bookmarklet.

There are quite a few such calculators on the internet, and this calculator contains no new ideas—it works like all the others: it calculates speed based on the user's VRAM bandwidth. But as it turned out, simply dividing one number by another (model weight by GPU bandwidth) is not entirely correct. When I said that in reality my speed was different, the neural networks started introducing correction factors in the form of GPU efficiency (60-80%).

Read more

item.title: How AI reduces the risks of accidents
item.description:
Accidents leading to occupational injuries are considered a serious problem worldwide, including in Russia. Often, such incidents result in either the loss of the worker's ability to work or a fatal outcome. The introduction of AI into the video monitoring system for a construction site allows reducing the probability of accidents at the facility. Based on statistical data, let's examine how this happens.

I decided to start with the construction sector because I know it very well and believe it is one of the important areas for AI application. Here, besides the construction process itself, the process of monitoring objects, personnel, and equipment is important. Modern systems work with several tools:

item.title: Qwen4: Architecture of the Future
item.description:
We need to clear things up right away, because there's confusion around the name. There is no full-fledged Qwen4. There is Qwen3.8-Flash‑Next — a model that the Qwen team itself calls "an experimental version of the architecture that will form the basis of Qwen4."

On August 26, 2026, the internet forgot about everything for a couple of hours. "Meet Qwen3.8-Flash, a multimodal MoE and an early preview of the Qwen4 architecture, now open‑weight!" And the numbers… 125 billion parameters in total. Plus another 51 billion as a separate layer. And only 6 billion are activated per token.

The first thought was: that can't be right.

item.title: Three-phase protection of your AI agents from modern threats with detailed analysis based on the OGL‑Mini security model
item.description:
The LLM boom has not only created new opportunities, but also a new generation of attacks. Over two years, we've seen real attacks on agents: one malicious email and Copilot leaks client payment data, one fake GitHub issue and the CI/CD pipeline is compromised, one carefully crafted prompt and the AI agent executes remote code on your machine. This is no longer theory, but attacks on Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI Atlas, Claude Code, and Apple Intelligence documented by researchers in 2025-2026.

Attacks are becoming more sophisticated: attackers disguise malicious instructions as XML policies, encrypt them in base64, insert invisible characters, and even hide jailbreaks in poetry. Built-in LLM filters miss up to 76% of such attacks.

This means a different approach is needed—lightweight, fast (so as not to slow down the agent), and understandable (so you know why the request was blocked). And crucially, it must work without external API calls, inside your infrastructure. Because in the era of zero-click attacks, trusting security to a cloud provider that lets almost everything through is at least risky.

In this article, we'll break down the main types of attacks and look at an example of how to build basic protection using the OGL-Mini security model.

Read more
